children: By David Uberti and Aaron Kuriloff
LARCHMONT, N.Y.-Jay Davis can't escape them.

He hears helicopters while working in his home office. He hears them when walking through a nearby park overlooking Long Island Sound. Most annoyingly, he hears them when he and his wife share meals in the enclosed porch adjoining their house in this New York City suburb, interrupting them mid-sentence and drowning out dinnertime viewing of "Wheel of Fortune."

Forget buying a vowel. Davis thought he had already bought some peace and quiet. "I have to put the closed captions on so I can see what's happening on the screen," the 53-year-old realtor and attorney said. "I don't want to continue to live like this."

Davis knows the noise is a champagne problem. In Westchester County, home to bedroom communities for Wall Street and Big Law, many problems are. But that dynamic-coupled with where the surge in traffic has been going-is part of what is spurring finger-pointing toward the skies.

Many of the choppers are heading to the Hamptons. Flyers' attempts to beat traffic and get a few more hours at the exclusive summer enclave are rattling the windows of people who believed they had earned a slice of suburban tranquility.

"One time I thought I had a helicopter in my driveway," said Nancy Monzidelis, a longtime Larchmont resident who has contacted the Federal Aviation Administration to no avail. "It's not as peaceful as it was before."

The annoyance has set off an unusual type of class warfare in the corner of Westchester known as the Sound Shore, where homes routinely fetch over $1 million and the sounds of summer typically include the flap of sailcloth, the crackle of a firepit and the bark of a coyote. Call it the 1% vs. the rest of the single-digiters, the uber-rich against the not-quite-rich-enough.

No one is alleging that the flight paths are illegal. But the flyovers are leaving some locals side-eying their comrades at Manhattan's white-shoe firms. One investment banker, who downloaded two mobile apps to track air traffic, wondered if hedge-fund and private-equity honchos are to blame following a yearslong runup in financial markets.

"Maybe some people are doing very well so they can afford a helicopter. Good for them," added Patrick Bucquet, a software engineer in Mamaroneck. "Of course they can travel to the Hamptons. But maybe they can take another route."

After moving from France over a decade ago, Bucquet has come to love traditional American barbecues on his deck-except for fly-bys on summer Fridays and Sundays that seem to arrive as often as every 15 minutes.

"If you're in the middle of a very interesting conversation, it just breaks the flow," said Bucquet, whose wife is less bothered. "Some people are more sensitive to noise than others. I'm probably in that group of people."

On a recent Friday evening at a Westchester yacht club, roughly a dozen choppers flew by in a two-hour stretch as members sipped rum cocktails on a waterside deck. One finance pro compared the sound to a Chinook military transport helicopter.
"It's giving me 'Nam flashbacks," a Larchmont resident added recently on the social-media platform NextDoor, where neighbors-behaving-badly content may as well be aviation fuel.
From the other side of Westchester in Yonkers, another user replied, "As a Vietnam Veteran myself I enjoy the flyovers. Welcome home."

New York City residents live with an ambient soundtrack of emergency sirens, subway screeches and I'm-walking-here arguments. A trio of airports add a near-constant hum of commercial jets. But even in the city and its immediate suburbs, it is helicopters used by the likes of police, travelers and news crews that often draw complaints.
The difference in southern Westchester is "you have a lot more quiet than you do than if you were living in the city," said Mateo Lallemand, a sophomore at Rye Country Day School.

The 16-year-old this year built an app that cross-references noise picked up from a microphone nearby his house against an FAA registry and the flight-tracking platform FlightRadar24. He modeled his system, which spits out the aircraft's operator, tail number and heading, on Ukrainian tools to track incoming Russian attacks.
The Ukrainian system is triggered by the sound of a missile or drone, Lallemand said. "But in our case, it's a helicopter."

The data show many Hamptons-bound flights operated by companies such as Flexjet traveling at around 1,000 feet, a fraction of the average cruising altitudes they advertise. Lallemand shared the data with his congressman, Rep. George Latimer, highlighting how the FAA in previous instances has prescribed routes that avoid residential areas.
Latimer said in a statement his team has engaged with FAA staff in studying the issue and investigating solutions. "The residents have a legitimate concern that cannot be ignored."

Safety is part of the reason so many choppers are flying so low, said Eli Flint, president of Flexjet's helicopter division. After an Army helicopter and passenger jet collided last year over Washington, killing dozens, air-traffic controllers have directed pilots to make more space for commercial airlines heading toward airports like LaGuardia.
"That's why we're at 700 to 1,000 feet," Flint said, adding that manufacturers are trying to develop new parts and equipment that dim noise. "We know it's an issue."

In Westchester, the helicopter criticisms have grown loud enough that they are drawing criticisms of their own. "These people around here complain about not having anything to complain about," said five-decade Mamaroneck resident Bonnie J. Lasek.

Lasek, whose family long owned a textile business that supplied Ralph Lauren and other major brands, summered in the Hamptons and nearby Fire Island for years. She's not a good flyer and has always driven.
"If somebody has the means to go to the Hamptons in a helicopter, God bless them," Lasek said. "You should just thank God you can hear them."
